item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Directional solidification using the Bridgman process instead of conventional casting
item.processing: Bridgman process with mold withdrawal speed of 3 mm/min through a water-cooled baffle
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C, annealed at 900 °C for 50 h
item.structure_change: Elongated grains in the direction of load, compared to polycrystalline microstructure with grain boundaries across the stress orientation
item.property_change: Ultimate tensile strength increased by a factor of 1.5–1.8 at room temperature to 700 °C; standard deviation of UTS reduced from 50 MPa to 16 MPa at room temperature
item.attributed_mechanism: Avoiding grain boundaries inclined at 45° to the loading direction eliminates shear stresses along weaker boundaries
quotes: Directional solidification (DS) showed an improvement in two ways as compared to conventional casting (CC).
On one hand, DS-samples scattered much less, as standard deviation of particularly ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and also strain to failure (ε f ) were reduced strongly for each temperature level
On the other hand, the most important improvement was the increase of UTS in case of the DS-samples by a factor of 1.5–1.8 in the range of room temperature up to 700 °C.

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Addition of 1.0 at.% Molybdenum (Mo) on the expense of Aluminum
item.processing: Vacuum induction melting, Bridgman directional solidification, homogenization at 1220 °C for 20 h, annealing at 900 °C for 50 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C
item.structure_change: γ′-precipitates changed from cuboidal with rounded corners to spherical shape; Heusler type phase remained needle-like
item.property_change: Ultimate tensile strength lowered compared to the base alloy under the same heat treatment conditions
item.attributed_mechanism: Round morphology of γ′-particles contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior
quotes: While the base alloy showed cuboidal particles with rounded corners, the Mo-alloy exhibited spherical, and the Hf-alloy showed cubic, sharp-cornered precipitates.
Under the same heat treatment conditions, Mo addition lowered the ultimate tensile strength of the base alloy due to the more round morphology of γ′-particles.
The worst behavior was exhibited by the Mo-containing alloy

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy). Intervention: Addition of 1.0 at.% Molybdenum (Mo) on the expense of Aluminum. Processing: Vacuum induction melting, Bridgman directional solidification, homogenization at 1220 °C for 20 h, annealing at 900 °C for 50 h. Test conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C. Structure change: γ′-precipitates changed from cuboidal with rounded corners to spherical shape; Heusler type phase remained needle-like. Property change: Ultimate tensile strength lowered compared to the base alloy under the same heat treatment conditions. Mechanism: Round morphology of γ′-particles contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior. Evidence: measured. Quote: "While the base alloy showed cuboidal particles with rounded corners, the Mo-alloy exhibited spherical, and the Hf-alloy showed cubic, sharp-cornered precipitates."

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Addition of 0.5 at.% Hafnium (Hf) on the expense of Aluminum
item.processing: Vacuum induction melting, Bridgman directional solidification, homogenization at 1140 °C for 20 h, annealing at 900 °C for 50 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C
item.structure_change: γ′-precipitates became cubic with sharp corners; Heusler type phase changed to spherical shape and accumulated at grain boundaries
item.property_change: Ultimate tensile strength increased compared to the base alloy; tests were very reproducible with little scatter
item.attributed_mechanism: The Hf-containing alloy showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase
quotes: An amount of 0.5 at.% hafnium sharpened the corners of the γ′-particles and lead to a spherical Heusler type phase.
The Hf-containing alloy, however, showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase.
First of all, various tests at the same temperature were very reproducible with only a little scatter.

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Annealing treatment changed from 900 °C/50 h to 950 °C/100 h
item.processing: Annealing at 950 °C for 100 h after homogenization
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C
item.structure_change: γ′-particle size increased from 200 nm to 400 nm; Heusler type volume fraction increased from 3% to 9%
item.property_change: Samples showed brittle fracture behavior at room temperature, 600 °C, and 700 °C; large scattering occurred regarding strain to failure
item.attributed_mechanism: The Heusler type phase content rose three times higher, causing the ultimate tensile strength to fall down drastically
quotes: Samples tested at room temperature showed a brittle fracture behavior, as well as specimens tested at 600 and 700 °C.
In the important temperature range the yield strength of the base alloy overran IN 617 by a factor of about 1.7 at 700 °C and 1.5 at 800 °C.
If the Heusler type phase content rose three times higher in the case of the base alloy, the ultimate tensile strength fell down drastically.

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Annealing treatment changed from 950 °C/100 h to 900 °C/50 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C
item.structure_change: Heusler type volume fraction reduced from 9% to 3%; γ′-particles remained smaller (200 nm vs 400 nm)
item.property_change: Higher ultimate tensile strength, higher strain to failure, and less scatter compared to the 950 °C/100 h treatment
item.attributed_mechanism: The desirable behavior was due to the volume content of Heusler type phase that was drastically reduced from 9% to 3%
quotes: Annealing at 900 °C/50 h did in fact lead to smaller precipitates, but these samples exhibited a higher ultimate tensile strength, higher strain to failure and less scatter.
The reason for this desirable behavior was due to the volume content of Heusler type phase that was drastically reduced from 9% to 3% after annealing at 900 °C/50 h
The annealing treatment of 900 °C/50 h for the base alloy lead to a similar mechanical behavior to that of the Hf-containing alloy

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Comparison of polycrystalline (conventionally cast) vs. directionally solidified microstructure
item.processing: Conventional casting vs. Bridgman process (3 mm/min)
item.structure_change: Conventional casting exhibits grain boundaries across the orientation of external stress; DS has elongated grains parallel to load
item.property_change: At 800 °C and 900 °C, the improvement by DS processing was only small (factor of 1.1 and 1.0 respectively)
item.attributed_mechanism: Grain boundaries play a strong role in weakening the material at higher temperatures; avoiding them eliminates shear stresses
quotes: Surprisingly, at higher temperatures of 800 and 900 °C the improvement by DS processing was only small (a factor of 1.1 and 1.0 respectively for 800 and 900 °C).
As a material itself has quite good creep properties, for example in the case of superalloys, the grain boundaries play a strong role in weakening the material at higher temperatures.
Avoiding grain boundaries inclined at 45° by the loading direction, shear stresses along these weaker boundaries can be eliminated

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Addition of 1.0 at.% Mo and 0.5 at.% Hf compared to base alloy
item.processing: All alloys processed via Bridgman, homogenized, and annealed at 900 °C/50 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests in the range of 600–900 °C
item.structure_change: Mo-alloy has round γ′-particles; Hf-alloy has sharp-cornered cubic γ′-particles and spherical Heusler phase
item.property_change: At 600–800 °C, the Hf-containing alloy showed the best mechanical properties, while the Mo-containing alloy exhibited the worst behavior
item.attributed_mechanism: Good high-temperature tensile properties occurred in the case of cubic precipitates, assumed that the Heusler type phase content was kept quite low
quotes: Between 700 and 800 °C, and also at 600 °C, there was a clear order: The worst behavior was exhibited by the Mo-containing alloy, the base alloy had a remarkably higher strength and the best mechanical properties could be observed in the case of the Hf-containing alloy.
Consequently, good high-temperature tensile properties occurred in the case of cubic precipitates, assumed that the Heusler type phase content was kept quite low.
The Hf-containing alloy, however, showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase.

item.base_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base alloy)
item.intervention: Comparison with commercial alloys Inconel 617 and Alloy 800 H
item.processing: Polycrystalline base alloy compared to commercial alloys
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests from room temperature to 900 °C
item.property_change: UTS of base alloy exceeded Alloy 800 H over the whole temperature range and exceeded IN 617 at 800 °C by a factor of 1.2; Yield strength overran IN 617 by a factor of 1.7 at 700 °C
quotes: In the important temperature range between 700 and 800 °C, UTS of the base alloy was equal in the beginning and even exceeded IN 617 at 800 °C by a factor of 1.2.
In the important temperature range the yield strength of the base alloy overran IN 617 by a factor of about 1.7 at 700 °C and 1.5 at 800 °C.

While the base alloy showed UTS exceeding that of Alloy 800 H over the whole temperature range, it was very similar or only a little worse than the UTS of the alloy Inconel 617 at temperatures up to 700 °C.
